Of course! While the `caption` package is the modern and recommended way to customize captions, you can achieve left-aligned captions without it by manually constructing the caption.

The standard `\caption` command is designed for centered text. To bypass this, we will create our own "caption" using a `\parbox` or a `\minipage`. This gives us full control over the alignment.

### The Manual Method: Using a `\parbox`

This method involves three key steps inside your `table` environment:
1.  **`\refstepcounter{table}`**: This manually increments the table counter (so you get "Table 2" after "Table 1") and sets the anchor for `\label` and `\ref`. This is the most important part to make referencing work correctly.
2.  **A `\parbox` or `\minipage`**: This creates a box of a specified width that will contain our caption text. We will set its width to `\linewidth` to match the text width.
3.  **`\raggedright`**: This is the command we place inside the box to make the text left-aligned.

---

### Complete Example

Here is a complete, compilable LaTeX example. The caption is placed **above** the table, which is the standard typographic convention for tables.

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lipsum} % For generating dummy text

\begin{document}

\lipsum[1]

\begin{table}[ht]
  % --- Start of manual left-aligned caption ---
  \refstepcounter{table} % 1. Increment the table counter and set ref anchor
  \label{tab:manual_table} % 3. Add the label for referencing
  \parbox{\linewidth}{%
    \raggedright % 2. Set the alignment to left-aligned
    \textbf{Table \thetable:} This is a very long table caption designed to demonstrate that the text will wrap and remain left-aligned without using the caption package.
  }
  % --- End of manual caption ---
  
  \vspace{6pt} % Add a little vertical space between caption and table
  
  \centering % Center the tabular environment itself
  \begin{tabular}{ll}
    \hline
    Header 1 & Header 2 \\
    \hline
    Data 1   & Data 2   \\
    Data 3   & Data 4   \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

As you can see in Table~\ref{tab:manual_table}, the caption is aligned to the left margin.

\lipsum[2]

% For comparison, here is a standard table caption
\begin{table}[ht]
  \centering
  \caption{This is a standard, centered caption to show the default behavior.}
  \label{tab:standard_table}
  \begin{tabular}{ll}
    \hline
    Header 1 & Header 2 \\
    \hline
    Data A   & Data B   \\
    Data C   & Data D   \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\end{document}
```

### Explanation of the Code

*   `\begin{table}[ht]` : Starts the floating table environment.
*   `\refstepcounter{table}` : This is the crucial command that `\caption` normally runs behind the scenes. It increases the `table` counter by one.
*   `\label{tab:manual_table}`: This must come **after** `\refstepcounter` to work correctly. It allows you to reference the table with `\ref{tab:manual_table}`.
*   `\parbox{\linewidth}{...}`: Creates a container for our caption. `\linewidth` makes the box as wide as the current text block.
*   `\raggedright`: This command, placed inside the `\parbox`, switches from justified text to left-aligned (ragged-right) text.
*   `\textbf{Table \thetable:}`: This manually creates the "Table 1:" part. `\thetable` prints the current value of the `table` counter. We make it bold to mimic the standard look.
*   `\vspace{6pt}`: Adds a small amount of vertical space to separate the caption from the table data.
*   `\centering`: This centers the `tabular` environment on the page, which is usually desired. It does not affect the caption text, which is inside its own `\parbox`.

### Alternative: Using a `minipage`

A `minipage` works almost identically to a `\parbox` and is sometimes preferred. The syntax is slightly different.

```latex
\begin{table}[ht]
  \refstepcounter{table}
  \label{tab:minipage_table}
  \begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
    \raggedright
    \textbf{Table \thetable:} This caption is inside a minipage and is also left-aligned.
  \end{minipage}
  
  \vspace{6pt}
  
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{cc}
    \hline
    Col A & Col B \\
    \hline
    1 & 2 \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

### Important Caveat: Why This Isn't Recommended

While the method above works perfectly, it's important to understand why the **`caption` package** is the standard solution.

1.  **Simplicity & Readability**: The `caption` package separates content from formatting. Your source code remains clean.
2.  **Flexibility**: You can change the alignment for all tables globally with one command in your preamble, rather than editing every single table.
3.  **Advanced Features**: The package provides many other features, like controlling spacing, fonts, styles, and handling captions for subfigures.

For completeness, here is how you would achieve the same result with the `caption` package.

```latex
% Add this to your preamble
\usepackage[justification=raggedright, singlelinecheck=false]{caption}

% Then, in your document, just use the standard \caption command
\begin{table}[ht]
  \centering
  \caption{This caption is automatically left-aligned thanks to the caption package.}
  \label{tab:package_table}
  \begin{tabular}{ll}
     \hline
     Data X & Data Y \\
     \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}
```
*   `justification=raggedright`: Aligns all caption text to the left.
*   `singlelinecheck=false`: Ensures that even short, single-line captions are left-aligned instead of being centered.
